On 2023-05-22, the User shared an explanation stating that SRAS assumes fixed capital in the short run, while firms can increase utilization of existing production factors; higher goods prices can encourage more production, whereas higher raw-material prices or wages shift SRAS left. On 2023-05-29, the User asked the Assistant to sort summaries of research abstracts into groups based on related findings, then rewrite them as headed paragraphs with studies in each paragraph ordered by publication year ascending.

Yin, Zheng, and Chen (2015) developed a panel-data model of institutional and technical factors affecting low-carbon economic development in China. They found a CO2-emissions Kuznets curve and a significant moderating effect of environmental regulation on the curve.

Li, Luo, and Wang (2019) studied the relationship among economic development, environmental sustainability, and human well-being in China. They found an inverted-N relationship between the carbon intensity of human well-being and economic growth, with GDP-per-capita turning points of 850 yuan and 110,000 yuan. They recommended environmental policies to offset unintended environmental harm and coordinated planning and development between adjacent provinces.

Liu, Qu, and Zhao (2019) examined whether China's development follows the Environmental Kuznets Curve and Pollution Haven hypotheses. They found a reverse-U relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions and an inverted-N relationship between foreign direct investment and CO2 emissions.

He and Lin (2019) used a panel smooth transition autoregression model to examine regional differences in China's Environmental Kuznets Curve. Pollution emissions and energy intensities decreased stepwise from western to eastern China; income's effect on pollution emissions was nonlinear, and energy intensity followed an inverted-U EKC.

Zhou, Wang, and Wang (2019) assessed how urbanization subsystems affect CO2 emissions in the Yangtze River Delta. Economic and spatial urbanization were positively associated with emissions; population urbanization had opposing effects; and social urbanization was negatively correlated with emissions.

Xu et al. (2020) studied noise pollution and economic development using monitoring data from 111 Chinese cities covering 1991–2017. They found an inverted-N relationship nationally, regional variation, and an association between tertiary-industry development and increased noise pollution.

Chen et al. (2020) used corrected NPP-VIIRS nighttime-light data to measure CO2 emissions at the city scale in China and examine the Environmental Kuznets Curve. They found that the city-scale EKC exists and that emissions vary by region.

Li et al. (2020) analyzed the Environmental Kuznets Curve and determinants of pollution-emission efficiency in Chinese provinces using data from 2005–2016. Provinces with low pollution emissions were mainly north of the Yangtze River. Important determinants included environmental regulation, industrial transfer, the output share of heavily polluting industries, energy-consumption structure, and energy-use efficiency.

Shahbaz, Shafiullah, Khalid, and Song (2020) analyzed the relationship between energy consumption and economic growth in Chinese provinces. They found nonlinear unit-root behavior in both variables, nonlinear cointegration between them, and mixed causal relationships according to Granger-causality analysis.

Wang et al. (2021) constructed differentiated energy Kuznets curves and a Cobb-Douglas production function using provincial time-series data to study mainland China's economic development. They found substantial provincial differences in EKC starting points, inflection points, and evolution trajectories.

Lu et al. (2021) applied the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis to the relationship between the carbon intensity of human well-being and economic development in eight Chinese economic zones during 1997–2015. Seven of the eight zones showed advances toward sustainability beginning between 2012 and 2015.

He et al. (2021) examined differences in the Environmental Kuznets Curve among pollutants and regions in China. They found different curve forms and turning points across cases and identified three regulations as effective for balancing urban emission reductions with long-term economic growth.

Ahmad, Jabeen, and Wu (2021) examined how foreign direct investment inflows and income affect CO2 emissions across Chinese provinces at different development levels. They found that FDI inflows and income promoted environmental sustainability; FDI had a Pollution Halo effect in 15 provinces and a Pollution Haven effect in seven provinces.

Liu et al. (2022) examined spatial variation and graded countermeasures for controlling children's blood lead levels in China using reported data. They concluded that urgent prevention and control strategies are needed in undeveloped areas.

Dai et al. (2022) tested the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis for the Weihe River basin using land footprint as an indicator of environmental degradation. They found that ecological measures can affect the curve's shape and cause the decoupling point to occur earlier.
Guo et al. (2022) studied GDP and transport-sector carbon emissions in 30 Chinese provinces and found an inverted-U relationship between them.

Chen et al. (2022) examined carbon-emission changes from residential and commercial building operations in 30 Chinese provinces using the carbon Kuznets curve model. More than three-quarters of samples fit the model; most curves were inverted-U shaped. At the total-emission scale, residential and commercial buildings accounted for 93% and 90%, respectively, as reported in the abstract.

Yilanci, Cutcu, and Cayir (2022) tested the Environmental Kuznets Curve using fishing-grounds footprint as an environmental-degradation indicator for China from 1961–2017. They found long-run evidence supporting the EKC and recommended common regional and global fishing policies and environmentally harmless technologies throughout fishery production.
